title: Bash Quiz
description: Review the 12 starter lessons. The questions name the example to revisit. Take your time, use the lessons, and read the reason after each answer.

questions.question: printf writes formatted text. %s inserts a string and backslash-n ends the line. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: printf puts the greeting into its %s slot. The format supplies the newline. Use a fixed format string so data is not mistaken for formatting.

questions.question: A variable assignment has no spaces around equals. Dollar-name reads the value. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The assignment stores text under name. The quoted expansion keeps it as one value. Quote variable expansions so spaces stay inside one value.

questions.question: Double parentheses with a dollar sign evaluate integer arithmetic. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: Arithmetic expansion works out 3 + 2 and inserts the result 5. Bash arithmetic uses whole numbers, not decimal fractions.

questions.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
score=8
if [[ "$score" -ge 5 ]]; then
 printf 'Pass\n'
else
 printf 'Try again\n'
fi
questions.question: [[ ... ]] tests a rule. -ge means greater than or equal for whole numbers. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The -ge test succeeds for 8. Bash runs the then commands. Use spaces inside [[ and ]] and finish the block with fi.

questions.question: A Bash array keeps indexed values. Its first position is zero. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The array has cat at zero and dog at one. Braces select the second value. Braces are needed around an indexed variable expansion.

questions.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
for n in 1 2 3; do
 printf '%s\n' "$n"
done
questions.question: A for loop repeats its body for each word in a list. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The for list has three words. Each pass prints its current word. Use "$@" or quoted array expansion when looping over values with spaces.

questions.question: A function groups commands. $1 is its first input. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The first function input becomes $1. printf inserts Ravi into the greeting. Function inputs are positional; quote them when reading.

questions.question: case chooses commands from text patterns. ;; ends one branch. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The green pattern matches, so that branch prints Go. End the whole choice with esac.

questions.question: ${name:-Guest} uses Guest when name is unset or empty. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The variable is empty. The :- form therefore supplies Guest. The colon makes an empty value use the fallback too.

questions.question: ${#name} gives the length of the variable value. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The # length form counts the four characters in Asha. For these examples use simple English letters so character counting is clear.

questions.question: A command returns an exit status. Zero usually means success. $? reads the last status. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The subshell returns status 3. Saving $? immediately preserves that status. Read $? immediately; the next command replaces it.

questions.question: The # expansion removes a matching prefix from a value. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The # prefix form removes notes from the front, leaving .txt. This edits the displayed text value; it does not rename a file.
